overview: Across the year, two reports drew the most mentions: Delivering the Suburban Rail Loop (August 2026), which prompted documents and select committee motions over the rail improvement charge on fares, and Maintaining State Roads (September), debated in both chambers. Other recurring threads were the IBAC Amendment Bills borrowing Auditor-General powers, integrity agency funding, school upgrades, out-of-home care, Preventing Youth Crime, the energy transition and state finances.

issues.label: Suburban Rail Loop report and rail improvement charge
issues.note: Delivering the Suburban Rail Loop prompted documents and select committee motions over a 1 per cent fare charge and a claimed $1 billion saving.

issues.label: Integrity agencies: funding, independence and IBAC powers
issues.note: A joint IBAC, Ombudsman and Auditor-General funding paper, IBAC bills borrowing Auditor-General powers, disputes over the office's independence and audit coverage of new bodies.

issues.label: Maintaining State Roads and road debates
issues.note: Tabled 9 September; both chambers heard that 48 per cent of state roads were poor or very poor, with funding and quality assurance concerns.

issues.label: State finances, debt and major projects findings
issues.note: Members cited findings on the State's annual financial report, debt and deficits, major projects cost increases and the Commonwealth Games budget.

issues.label: Reports on schools, TAFE, care and youth crime
issues.note: Delivering School Upgrade Projects, Free TAFE, Out-of-Home Care Services and Preventing Youth Crime were cited to criticise or defend service delivery.

issues.label: Renewable energy transition risk findings
issues.note: Members cited the December 2025 Managing the Transition to Renewable Energy report on Yallourn's 2028 closure, supply risks and delayed projects.

debates.gist: Council bill debate: a Greens amendment on independent IBAC funding cited the joint paper by IBAC, the Auditor-General's Office and the Ombudsman; the government described IBAC powers comparable to the Auditor-General's; another member cited the Auditor-General's fare charge report.

Council debate on Bev McArthur's motion noting the Auditor-General's Maintaining State Roads findings, including 48 per cent of state roads in poor or very poor condition; supporters cited the report, while government members pointed to repair crews and extra investment.

Assembly matter of public importance and question time on road maintenance after the Maintaining State Roads report was tabled: opposition members cited findings on condition, defects and funding, and a government member raised an earlier Premier's attempt to sack the Auditor-General.

Council debate on David Davis's motion for a select committee on the Auditor-General's Suburban Rail Loop report: supporters said Victorians deserve answers on the fare charge, while government members said it would duplicate the independent 171-page audit.

Council debate on Evan Mulholland's documents motion arising from the Auditor-General's Suburban Rail Loop report: opposition members cited the rail improvement charge and unfunded savings, while a government member stressed the Auditor-General's independence and said the government would not oppose the motion.

Assembly second reading speeches on the IBAC Amendment Bill: members described follow-the-money powers giving IBAC powers comparable to the Auditor-General's, and one recalled the Kennett government's attempts to alter the Auditor-General's powers.

Council question time and members statements the day after the Auditor-General's Suburban Rail Loop report: opposition members cited a 1 per cent fare levy expected to raise about $8 billion by 2062, while a government member thanked the Auditor-General.

Council statements on the day the Suburban Rail Loop report was tabled: members called its revelations bombshells and extraordinary, and one cited a fare tax expected to raise about $8 billion by 2062 and government knowledge of overruns.

Council debate on a documents motion seeking departmental advice on recommendations 8 and 9 of the Auditor-General's Protecting Victoria's Biodiversity report; the government did not oppose it, and one member cited the finding that the department could not show it was halting species decline.

Assembly second reading speeches on the dangerous goods bill in which members cited the Auditor-General's Delivering School Upgrade Projects findings on cost blowouts and school condition, and one called for an account of Auditor-General oversight of successor companies.

Council second reading debate on the Entities Legislation Amendment Bill: members cited Auditor-General findings that waste diversion targets are off track, the public service is under-resourced and the operating budget was in deficit in December, in arguing against cuts and for amendments.

Council debate on a reference to the Integrity and Oversight Committee on integrity agency funding: members cited the February joint paper by the Ombudsman, IBAC and the Auditor-General's Office, praised the Auditor-General's work, and discussed why the Auditor-General answers to a different committee.

VIC-0001.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Preventing Youth Crime report, handed down the previous day, saying 236,727 Victorians (3.3 per cent of the population) were victims of crime between June 2024 and June 2025.

VIC-0002.summary: Argued integrity agencies need funding set independently of government, and cited the joint IBAC, Auditor-General's Office and Ombudsman paper Advancing Budget Transparency for Victoria's Core Integrity Agencies, one recommendation of which an amendment would implement for IBAC.

VIC-0003.summary: Described the bill as giving IBAC powers comparable to the Victorian Auditor-General's, including follow-the-money powers over third-party and private subcontractors, with definitions drawing on the Audit Act 1994.

VIC-0004.summary: Cited last month's Auditor-General report as showing a secret tax on public transport, offering it as an example of the behaviour the IBAC bill is meant to expose.

VIC-0005.summary: Claimed governments have systemically underfunded integrity agencies, including IBAC, the Ombudsman and the Auditor-General's Office, and said the amendments would let the public see when that happens.

VIC-0006.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's warning about the risks of consistently outsourcing work traditionally done by public servants, including deskilling the public service, in arguing that stripping out government capability leads to paying private firms for it.

VIC-0007.summary: Auditor-General's reports Preventing Youth Crime (ordered to be published) and Public Lottery Licence Extension (released 16 September 2026) tabled by the Clerk among documents under Acts of Parliament.

VIC-0008.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report released that day as saying the government spent over $40 million in a decade while 70 per cent of youth participants reoffend within six months, and said Latrobe Valley youth crime keeps rising.

VIC-0009.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report from two weeks earlier for the claim that the current Premier, as roads minister, cut the road maintenance budget by $200 million in 2021–22, which the member said began the roads' decline.

VIC-0010.summary: Auditor-General's report Preventing Youth Crime, September 2026, tabled by the Clerk and ordered to be published.

VIC-0011.summary: Cited Auditor-General findings that the Commonwealth Games budget was unrealistically low and the business case inadequate, and that SRL East was unlikely to meet the announced budget and timetable, with the $34.5 billion estimate possibly over a billion short.

VIC-0012.summary: Said the government did not need a Victorian Auditor-General's Office report to know road conditions must improve, and pointed to announced measures such as supervised offenders supplementing crews to fix more potholes.

VIC-0013.summary: Supported the road maintenance motion, saying the Auditor-General's report shows poor road conditions in regional Victoria with more than half very poor, before turning to rebut earlier remarks by Labor members.

VIC-0014.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's findings that state roads rated poor or very poor rose from 39 per cent in 2021 to 48 per cent in 2024, with a growing backlog, insufficient funding and one in eight inspected works defective.

VIC-0015.summary: Said extra investment and crews now fixing roads respond to issues rightly identified in the Auditor-General's Maintaining State Roads report, and that Labor, if re-elected, would change the way roads are fixed.

VIC-0016.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Office report showing almost half of Victoria's roads in poor or very poor condition, alongside RACV's My Country Road 2026 survey placing four of the state's five worst roads in Western Victoria Region.

VIC-0017.summary: Moved a motion noting the Auditor-General's Maintaining State Roads findings: 48 per cent of state roads poor or very poor in 2024, up from 39 per cent in 2021, a growing backlog, insufficient funding and one in eight inspected works defective.

VIC-0018.summary: Raised, in a question to the roads minister, constituents' concern over the Auditor-General's Office finding that the City of Casey recorded the highest number of potholes in metropolitan Melbourne.

VIC-0019.summary: Recalled inheriting a housing portfolio in crisis as minister, citing an Auditor-General report that more than 10,000 department properties were uninhabitable, which the member attributed to Labor's lack of maintenance investment.

VIC-0020.summary: Spoke on the Auditor-General's Preventing Youth Crime report handed down that morning, calling it an independent assurance report to Parliament that the member said confirms the government's approach to youth crime is not working.

VIC-0021.summary: Described IBAC bill changes to the 'public body' and 'public officer' definitions, drawing on the Audit Act 1994, giving IBAC powers comparable to the Auditor-General's, in line with the Integrity and Oversight Committee's recommendation.

VIC-0022.summary: Auditor-General's report Public Lottery Licence Extension, September 2026, released on 16 September during a non-sitting period, tabled by the Clerk and ordered to be published.

VIC-0023.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Delivering School Upgrade Projects report, released in June, including its finding that VSBA does not always recommend upgrade projects in line with its strategies for improving school conditions.

VIC-0024.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's 2018 report on Victoria Police property and exhibits, which found none of 15 audit reports from eight stations compliant, and asked the Premier to request a fresh audit.

VIC-0025.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Office report released that week as showing 47.98 per cent of the Hume region's roads in very poor condition, and argued the causes of road failure need thorough investigation.

VIC-0026.summary: Mentioned the Auditor-General's Office Suburban Rail Loop report in passing, in a list of matters the member said the government was distracting from.

VIC-0027.summary: Asked the roads minister about Auditor-General findings that the government cannot verify how defective road repairs are fixed, a quarter of routine maintenance works were non-compliant and one in eight were defective.

VIC-0028.summary: Auditor-General's report Maintaining State Roads (Volumes 1 and 2) tabled by the Clerk and ordered to be published.

VIC-0029.summary: Asked the energy minister why the department did not give the Auditor-General requested analysis of winter supply risks in the December 2025 report Managing the Transition to Renewable Energy, and whether the modelling will be released; also said wind projects were years behind.

VIC-0030.summary: Argued respecting the Auditor-General means engaging with reports and implementing recommendations to improve the Suburban Rail Loop, not using them to justify abandoning it, and acknowledged the Auditor-General found the original business case needed refinement.

VIC-0031.summary: Pointed to the Auditor-General's power to follow public money through complex delivery arrangements as the precedent for giving IBAC follow-the-money powers over private entities performing public functions.

VIC-0032.summary: Said follow-the-money powers would give IBAC powers comparable to the Auditor-General's to investigate corrupt conduct by third-party and private subcontractors linked to public functions.

VIC-0033.summary: Auditor-General's report Maintaining State Roads, September 2026 (Volumes 1 and 2), tabled by the Clerk and ordered to be published.

VIC-0034.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Office report Maintaining State Roads, tabled that day, saying 48 per cent of state roads are in poor or very poor condition, in a statement on the Budget Estimates report.

VIC-0035.summary: On a point of order in the road maintenance debate, sought to table the Auditor-General's Maintaining State Roads report, after another member said south-east roads were 'coming along quite great'.

VIC-0036.summary: Claimed the Auditor-General's report tabled that day uncovered that the Premier, as roads minister, promised things that were not true, and cited mounting reports from authorities such as the Auditor-General's Office.

VIC-0037.summary: Said the Auditor-General plays an important role, citing the report on a 'secret tax' on public transport, and quoted Maintaining State Roads: road condition is deteriorating and performance targets give no meaningful insight into it.

VIC-0038.summary: Cited Auditor-General figures that state roads rated poor or very poor rose from 39 per cent in 2021 to 48 per cent in 2024 and that the gap between defects identified and fixed more than doubled, and claimed the government sought to undermine the findings.

VIC-0039.summary: Said the Auditor-General's report tabled that day shows roads deteriorating faster than the government is fixing them, and that the department warned the government funding was insufficient to maintain or improve road condition.

VIC-0040.summary: Welcomed the opposition's appreciation of the Auditor-General's work, repeatedly asserted that no Premier from the government's side had sought to sack the Auditor-General, and cited an Australia Institute report on proposed cuts.

VIC-0041.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report finding 48 per cent of roads poor or very poor, noting its references to travel times, vehicle operating costs and accident risk, and said such road audits occur about every eight years.

VIC-0042.summary: Asked the roads minister about Auditor-General figures showing $487 million in extra maintenance funding this year falling to $225 million next year, and said the report shows 48 per cent of the road network in poor or very poor condition.

VIC-0043.summary: Opposed the proposed select committee on the Suburban Rail Loop report, arguing it would duplicate the Auditor-General's independent 171-page audit, identifies no gap in its work and shows political bias, and noting the Premier acknowledged insufficient transparency around the charge.

VIC-0044.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Office as acknowledging $1 billion of a claimed $2 billion Suburban Rail Loop saving was never funded, and said the whole cabinet knew of the 'secret tax', mocking Minister Dimopoulos's claim to have first heard of it in the Auditor-General's report.

VIC-0045.summary: Supported a select committee on the Auditor-General's Delivering the Suburban Rail Loop report, saying a project of this size needs serious consideration, with SRL East expected to cost up to $34.5 billion.

VIC-0046.summary: Opposed the Suburban Rail Loop select committee, saying the Premier axed the charge after the Auditor-General's report, praising the office's checks-and-balances role, and arguing the committee could show nothing not already in the report.

VIC-0047.summary: Supported a select committee on the Auditor-General's Suburban Rail Loop report, arguing the findings cannot be put aside, there should be no hidden taxes, and former ministers, the Premier and Deputy Premier should explain decisions.

VIC-0048.summary: Noted that Mr Batchelor had described the Auditor-General's Office report as detailed and candid and as making clear the secret tax levied was wrong, in speaking to the select committee motion.

VIC-0049.summary: Opposed the select committee as a political exercise, saying the Auditor-General's 171-page report by an independent officer was detailed and candid and showed a lack of transparency about the rail improvement charge, which is gone.

VIC-0050.summary: Moved a motion for a six-member select committee to report within 30 days on the Auditor-General's report Delivering the Suburban Rail Loop, tabled 26 August 2026, and to examine related matters arising from it.

VIC-0051.summary: Questioned whether Mrs McArthur had read the Auditor-General's Office report, saying it explains the term under debate and that Mr Mulholland had read it, and encouraged members to read it.

VIC-0052.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's 26 August report on a secret 1 per cent rail improvement charge added to public transport fares from 1 January 2025, and claimed it found the Premier's $1 billion Suburban Rail Loop saving largely fiction.

VIC-0053.summary: Said the government would not oppose the documents motion, and described the Auditor-General as an independent officer of Parliament who does not write reports to suit government or opposition, noting the 171-page report examined four public entities.

VIC-0054.summary: Moved a documents motion on the Auditor-General's Delivering the Suburban Rail Loop report, citing its finding of an unannounced 1 per cent 'rail improvement charge' on fares from 1 January 2025, modelled to raise about $8 billion, with $4.8 billion for SRL East.

VIC-0055.summary: Spoke on the Auditor-General's Maintaining State Roads report, tabled that day, calling it and the earlier Suburban Rail Loop report damning, and said Labor is not spending enough on roads and cannot properly manage what it does spend.

VIC-0056.summary: Opened a statement on the Auditor-General's Maintaining State Roads report, tabled that day, saying maintaining and building roads is one of the basic services government provides.

VIC-0057.summary: Financial Audit of the Auditor-General and the Victorian Auditor-General's Office 2026 (three documents) and the Auditor-General's Report 2025–26 tabled by the Clerk, alongside an IBAC report to the Attorney-General.

VIC-0058.summary: Claimed that Victorian Auditor-General's Office reports from the last 20 years show children do far worse when removed from families, while accepting that removing parental authority should be done extraordinarily carefully.

VIC-0059.summary: Business program listing an amended notice of motion in David Davis's name to establish a select committee to inquire into the Auditor-General's report Delivering the Suburban Rail Loop.

VIC-0060.summary: Recounted that the Auditor-General raised concerns about corruption in ambulance services in 1997, and that the Kennett government's later attempts to alter the Auditor-General's powers created significant challenges, as an example of what happens when independent bodies are marginalised.

VIC-0061.summary: Said the bill brings private contractors and subcontractors ('associated entities') within IBAC's reach using the same kind of definition the Auditor-General already works with, so IBAC can follow the money.

VIC-0062.summary: Said the bill's follow-the-money changes give IBAC powers comparable to the Victorian Auditor-General's over third-party and private subcontractors, amending 'public body' and 'public officer' definitions to include associated entities, drawing on the Audit Act 1994.

VIC-0063.summary: Auditor-General's Office Report 2025–26 tabled by the Clerk, together with an IBAC report to the Attorney-General for 2024.

VIC-0064.summary: Referred to the Auditor-General's report of the previous week when previewing the week's debate, claiming the budget papers do not contain the 'secret tax'.

VIC-0065.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Delivering the Suburban Rail Loop report on a tax put on in 2021 and expected to raise about $8 billion, and on announced savings not funded in the business case, while criticising state debt.

VIC-0066.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Office report revealing a secret tax on public transport fares to 2062 as the elephant in the room for the budget, and said the Auditor-General and Stephen Conroy had exposed the Suburban Rail Loop.

VIC-0067.summary: Financial Audit of the Victorian Auditor-General's Office for the year ended 30 June 2026 tabled by the Clerk under section 81(4) of the Audit Act 1994.

VIC-0068.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's findings that a secret tax on public transport fares, approved in 2021 and expected to raise $8 billion, was not disclosed in public documents, in arguing Victorians have reason to doubt government assurances.

VIC-0069.summary: Raised, in a question to the Premier, the Auditor-General's revelation that public transport fares rose an extra 1 per cent from January 2025 to help fund the Suburban Rail Loop, claiming frequent commuters pay over $3000 more a year.

VIC-0070.summary: Mentioned the Auditor-General in passing in a list of bodies, including IBAC and the Ombudsman, excluded from the mandate under the bill.

VIC-0071.summary: Thanked the Auditor-General for important work, after saying the Premier had outlined the government's position on the Suburban Rail Loop.

VIC-0072.summary: Raised, in a question to the Minister for Finance, the Auditor-General's revelation of an undisclosed 1 per cent tax on every public transport ticket since January 2025, projected to raise $8 billion by 2062 for SRL East.

VIC-0073.summary: Said the Auditor-General confirmed an undisclosed 1 per cent levy on public transport fares since January 2025, expected to raise about $8 billion by 2062 with $4.8 billion for SRL East, and that the Premier announced its scrapping only after exposure.

VIC-0074.summary: Drew the house's attention to the Auditor-General's report of the previous day, saying the government plans to take $8 billion from Victorians in a transport tax to backfill Suburban Rail Loop cost blowouts and underfunding.

VIC-0075.summary: Asked the Premier why a $1 billion Suburban Rail Loop saving was claimed from scrapping underground interchanges at Box Hill and Glen Waverley that the Auditor-General says were never funded.

VIC-0076.summary: Asked the Premier why an $8 billion tax was concealed for five years until the Auditor-General exposed it.

VIC-0077.summary: Referred in passing to the previous day's Auditor-General report on the 'secret tax' as an example of a government shrouded in secrecy, while complaining about being blocked from visiting Triple Zero as shadow minister.

VIC-0078.summary: Auditor-General's report Delivering the Suburban Rail Loop tabled by the Clerk and ordered to be published, among documents under Acts of Parliament.

VIC-0079.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's report that day on a secret 1 per cent levy in public transport fares as a contrast with the Premier's integrity pledges, then asked where the June quarter waiting list figures are and what the government does not want seen.

VIC-0080.summary: Quoted a February joint paper by the Ombudsman, IBAC Commissioner and Auditor-General saying integrity agencies must be transparently and appropriately funded, while arguing the government refuses to give them the resources they need.

VIC-0081.summary: Mentioned in passing that the Premier planned a flight to Canberra knowing the Victorian Auditor-General's Office report was due out that day, during a debate on Liberal Party policy.

VIC-0082.summary: Cited a Senate inquiry's record that a Victorian Auditor-General examination put the genuine cost of administration at between 28 cents and 93 cents, in criticising administration fees under the Melbourne City Link Act 1995.

VIC-0083.summary: Said the Auditor-General's Delivering the Suburban Rail Loop report, tabled that day, left the member flabbergasted, and argued the Premier should come clean about what was known of the 'secret tax' on fares if integrity is not optional.

VIC-0084.summary: Auditor-General's report Delivering the Suburban Rail Loop, August 2026, tabled by the Clerk and ordered to be published.

VIC-0085.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's finding of a secret tax levied since January 2025 on every bus and train user to help pay for the Suburban Rail Loop, rising 1 per cent a year, and asked how long Polwarth residents will pay it.

VIC-0086.summary: Said fare adjustments are reported every year before 1 January, and, out of respect for the Auditor-General's work, acknowledged DTF has accepted the Auditor-General's recommendation on improving communication to the community.

VIC-0087.summary: Raised, in a question to the Minister for Public Transport, the Auditor-General's finding that at least $1.6 billion of the Box Hill and Glen Waverley underground interchanges was never in the Suburban Rail Loop budget, after the government claimed a $1 billion saving.

VIC-0088.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Delivering the Suburban Rail Loop report as exposing a fare tax expected to cost about $8 billion by 2062, and said the Auditor-General confirmed in a briefing that the government knew in January the project was over budget.

VIC-0089.summary: Opened a statement on the Auditor-General's Office Suburban Rail Loop report, calling it a series of bombshells, pointing to pages 8 to 23, and saying it would be raised in the house again.

VIC-0090.summary: Opened a statement on the Auditor-General's Delivering the Suburban Rail Loop report, tabled that day, calling some of its revelations extraordinary while saying some may not surprise.

VIC-0091.summary: Welcomed the committee's recommendation for an Auditor-General review of the waste-to-energy regulatory framework, but criticised the rejection of other proposals, including a moratorium until the Auditor-General makes a finding.

VIC-0092.summary: Described the committee's term, including follow-up inquiries into Auditor-General's Office reports on gambling and liquor regulation and on local government financial and fraud controls, audits of the Auditor-General's office and the recommendation to reappoint the Auditor-General.

VIC-0093.summary: Cited a Victorian Auditor-General's Office report of a few years ago saying up to 40 per cent of public health respondents experienced burnout, alongside the 2024 People Matter survey, in a debate on nurse and midwife ratios.

VIC-0094.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's 2024 report as showing a significant increase over the last decade in patients having to stay 24 hours or more, describing the pressure on staff and poor patient outcomes.

VIC-0095.summary: Mentioned the Victorian Auditor-General's Office in passing, in a list of integrity bodies whose oversight arrangements the proposed Racing Integrity Commissioner arrangements are said to mirror.

VIC-0096.summary: Called on the government to explain what the bill's changes mean for freedom of information, Victorian Auditor-General's Office oversight, the Ombudsman and IBAC, procurement, borrowing, executive remuneration and public records.

VIC-0097.summary: Listed the Victorian Auditor-General's Office, with WorkSafe, the Ombudsman and IBAC, among bodies that periodically look at the corrections system and report on it.

VIC-0098.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's record of $1.24 billion accumulated impairment for roads and bridges at 30 June 2024, and an earlier audit identifying a growing maintenance backlog and declining service levels.

VIC-0099.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Commonwealth Games and major projects performance reports, claiming a secret rise in the Games budget from $2.6 to $3.6 billion and that budget paper 4 is no longer a reliable guide to major project costs.

VIC-0100.summary: Answered the member for Hawthorn's reference to the Auditor-General by saying the budget is there every year, and asked whether the opposition would rewrite budget paper 4 and what it promises instead.

VIC-0101.summary: Recalled the November 2023 report Gambling and Liquor Regulation in Victoria: A Follow up of Three Auditor-General Reports, and said the member remains passionate about the issue and has spoken on it before.

VIC-0102.summary: Spoke on the Auditor-General's report Reducing the Harm Caused by Distracted Drivers, submitted in June, which examined the distracted driver and seatbelt detection camera program, noting the Auditor-General acknowledges mobile phone use raises crash risk.

VIC-0103.summary: Opened a statement on the Auditor-General's audit Improving Bus Services by describing Victoria's bus plan as ambitious but light on detail, with a vision of Melbourne's buses becoming mass transit by 2031.

VIC-0104.summary: Cited the Auditor-General as stating the risk of a disorderly energy transition is almost certain with Yallourn closing in 2028, and that current generation and battery projects will not offset the closure from mid-2028.

VIC-0105.summary: Cited the recent Auditor-General report on school upgrades as finding that 29 per cent of upgrades had cost blowouts and 25 per cent were delayed, after saying schools that did the work themselves saved money.

VIC-0106.summary: Said the Auditor-General has warned that Victoria faces a significant risk of electricity shortfall after the expected closure of the Yallourn power station in 2028, with risks of blackouts and higher bills.

VIC-0107.summary: Supported the documents motion and, among examples of reviews, pointed to the Auditor-General's recent follow-up on bushfire preparedness, which the member called damning of the government.

VIC-0108.summary: Said the government does not oppose documents motions, describing the motion seeking departmental advice on recommendations 8 and 9 of the Auditor-General's Office report Protecting Victoria's Biodiversity.

VIC-0109.summary: Moved a documents motion citing the Auditor-General's Protecting Victoria's Biodiversity finding that the department could not demonstrate whether it was halting threatened species decline, and said the latest state of the environment report rated 26 of 42 biodiversity indicators poor.

VIC-0110.summary: Spoke on the Auditor-General's report Delivering School Upgrade Projects, saying the Victorian School Building Authority accepted all six recommendations and that the report identified its understanding of school conditions as a strength.

VIC-0111.summary: Cited a 2017 Victorian Auditor-General prediction that continuing trends would put over 91 per cent of roads in poor or very poor condition, saying that is where the state now is.

VIC-0112.summary: Heading for statements on the tabled Auditor-General's report Delivering School Upgrade Projects; no speech text recorded.

VIC-0113.summary: Auditor-General's reports tabled by the Clerk, including the Annual Plan 2026–27, Delivering School Upgrade Projects, a Service Victoria follow-up, Investing in Early Intervention Initiatives and Planning and Managing Drainage Schemes in Melbourne's Growth Areas.

VIC-0114.summary: Cited Delivering School Upgrade Projects, saying 11 of 18 Macedon Ranges government schools were in poor condition and upgrade decisions did not always follow prioritisation guidelines, and recalled an Auditor-General report that 10,000 public housing properties were nearing the end of usable life.

VIC-0115.summary: Described the Auditor-General's newly tabled report on progress implementing recommendations from a 2021 report as damning, saying it outlines a government rudderless on digital service delivery.

VIC-0116.summary: Claimed the Auditor-General found one Commonwealth Games cost blowout was a $2 billion contingency for industrial relations risks and cost escalations, approved in cabinet by the former and current Premiers, in support of the no-confidence motion.

VIC-0117.summary: Auditor-General's Annual Plan 2026–27, released on 24 June 2026 during a non-sitting period, tabled by the Clerk and ordered to be published.

VIC-0118.summary: Said, as minister, that the Auditor-General's bushfire report acknowledges strong government work on risk modelling, data capability and planning and calls for continual improvement and investment; a point of order from Melina Bath said the report found the data unreliable.

VIC-0119.summary: Put to the Minister for Environment the Auditor-General's June 2026 findings that fuel management is not shown to work, key data is unreliable and recommendations remain unimplemented, and asked for independently verified bushfire risk data before the next fire season.

VIC-0120.summary: Said Tinternvale Primary School was ranked top for poor condition in the previous day's Auditor-General's Office report Delivering School Upgrade Projects, in a constituency question on the school's needs.

VIC-0121.summary: Compared non-binding Land Access Panel advice to the Auditor-General's recommendations, saying agencies or government decide whether to adopt them.

VIC-0122.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's finding of serious weaknesses in administering forestry transition funding, including gaps in departmental records, problems showing how some eligibility decisions were verified and inadequate monitoring of long-term employment outcomes.

VIC-0123.summary: Said the Auditor-General's recent report on reducing bushfire risks acknowledges improvements since 2020 but finds key recommendations unresolved six years later, with concerns about risk modelling, fuel reduction, private land management and strategic fuel breaks.

VIC-0124.summary: Auditor-General's reports Delivering School Upgrade Projects and Improving Bus Services tabled by the Clerk and ordered to be published.

VIC-0125.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's Out-of-Home Care Services report finding that the 9353 children in care are not having needs fully met, sibling requirements are not met, and the department repeatedly advised government of constraints and sought funding.

VIC-0126.summary: Said the Auditor-General's Office report on free TAFE, tabled seven years after its introduction, delivered the verdict that it provides training for priority skills and delivers real benefits.

VIC-0127.summary: Cited the Auditor-General's school upgrades report as finding VSBA recommendations not in line with its strategies, not always transparent and based on informal processes including community pressure and political considerations, and pointed to the office's dashboard on school condition.

VIC-0128.summary: Thanked the Auditor-General and staff for their work, and cited Delivering School Upgrade Projects: 29 per cent of upgrades had cost blowouts, 25 per cent were delayed, poor-condition schools rose from 182 to 221, and three of 10 priority schools were not rated poor.
